name: Hollow-Sanctuary
specific_features: Lava tubes large enough to contain pressurized habitable environments
Subsurface microbial ecosystems in sealed cave pockets
description: Hollow-Sanctuary is a barren world whose unremarkable surface conceals a vast network of lava tubes, some large enough in diameter to house full-scale habitation modules with room to spare. The surface is standard regolith over basalt, cratered and dust-covered, offering nothing to distinguish it from a thousand similar bodies. Below, however, the tubes extend for hundreds of kilometers in interconnected networks, their smooth-walled passages sealed well enough to retain pockets of atmosphere that have persisted for millions of years, isolated environments where chemistry has proceeded along paths unavailable on the exposed surface.

The thin surface atmosphere is insufficient for unprotected human activity, but within the larger sealed tube sections, atmospheric pressure approaches breathable levels, the gas composition a mixture of volcanic outgassing products that have slowly accumulated over geological time. The temperature within the tubes is remarkably stable, the rock providing insulation that buffers the surface extremes into a narrow band just cool enough to require light heating. The silence underground is not the dead silence of vacuum but the living silence of enclosed space, the faint drip of mineral-laden water and the barely perceptible hiss of gas seeping through rock joints.

Microbial life thrives in the sealed tube sections, chemolithotrophic organisms that derive energy from the mineral-rich water percolating through the basalt. These communities have evolved in complete isolation from the surface for millions of years, their biochemistry diverging from any known baseline in ways that suggest the sealed environment has driven rapid evolutionary adaptation. Some tube sections contain microbial communities so dense that the walls are coated in visible biofilms, their metabolic activity contributing to the atmospheric composition of their sealed worlds in a miniature echo of planetary-scale biogeochemistry.

Hollow-Sanctuary has been identified as an ideal candidate for subsurface colonization, the lava tubes providing natural pressure vessels and radiation shielding that would cost billions to construct artificially. The sealed microbial ecosystems present both an opportunity and a complication, their scientific value arguing against the habitat conversion that would make colonization practical. Several tubes have been opened and converted to habitation use, their microbial communities relocated to laboratory containment before pressurization and warming. The planet's nickname among prospective colonists is the Sanctuary, a place where the hostile surface gives way to sheltered spaces that seem almost designed to welcome those who know where to look.
